    Performance Tips

    There are a few things you can do to make sure the tool performs well.

    First, process objects one at a time. The code 

    await
    s each encryption in turn. That keeps memory use low, because only one stream is copied at a time. For files with thousands of small objects you can encrypt in batches of, say, 50 with 
    Promise.all
    to go faster.

    Second, expect the file to grow a little. Each string and stream gains a 16-byte IV and up to 16 bytes of padding, and saving without object streams makes the cross-reference table bigger. A 4 KB file might become 8 KB, while a 5 MB file grows by only a few kilobytes.

    Next, don't encrypt twice for the check. The tool verifies the exact bytes it's going to download. Don't run 

    protectPdf
    again for the download, or the file will get a new random key and the check will no longer apply to it.

    Finally, release memory after big files. Call 

    doc.destroy()
    on PDF.js documents when you're done, as 
    verify
    does. Otherwise the worker keeps the parsed file in memory.

    Common Mistakes

    There are also a few things to avoid when you're building this tool.

    First, don't open the page over plain 

    http://
    . 
    crypto.subtle
    only exists in secure contexts. On 
    http://example.com
    or a 
    file://
    path, the code fails with "Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'digest')". Use 
    https://
    or 
    localhost
    .

    Don't use 

    Math.random()
    for keys or salts. It isn't designed for security, and its output can be predicted. Always use 
    crypto.getRandomValues()
    .

    You also shouldn't encrypt the encryption dictionary. If the 

    /U
    , 
    /O
    or 
    /Perms
    strings get encrypted, no reader can check a password. Encrypt the document first, then add the dictionary.

    Avoid saving with object streams. PDF-lib saves with object streams by default. With encryption, strings inside them would be encrypted twice. Pass 

    useObjectStreams: false
    .

    Also, don't forget 

    slice()
    when passing bytes to PDF.js. PDF.js transfers the buffer to its worker. Afterwards your original 
    Uint8Array
    is empty, and the download is a 0-byte file.

    Don't treat permissions as security. Restricting printing and copying is useful for honest readers, but it isn't protection. If the content must stay private, the open password is what matters.

    Don't protect a digitally signed PDF. Encrypting changes every byte that the signature covers, so the signature becomes invalid. Add the password first, then sign the protected file.

    And finally, make sure you and your users don't lose the password. With AES-256 there's no back door and no "forgot password" button. Tell your users to store the password somewhere safe.

    Conclusion

    In this tutorial, you built a browser-based tool that adds a password to a PDF with AES-256 encryption.

    You learned how PDF encryption is organized, how to hash a password with the PDF 2.0 algorithm, how to build the 

    U
    , 
    UE
    , 
    O
    , 
    OE
    and 
    Perms
    values with the Web Crypto API, how to encrypt every string and stream with PDF-lib, and how to check the result with PDF.js and qpdf.

    All of it runs in the browser, so the document stays on the user's device.

    You can try the full version of this tool, with page previews, AES-128 and RC4 options for very old readers, low-resolution-only printing, and more detailed permission choices at Protect PDF.

    If you want to extend your version, here are some ideas:

    • Add an Unlock tool that removes the password when the user knows it
    • Let users choose "print in low resolution only" (bit 3 without bit 12)
    • Protect several PDFs with the same password in one go
    • Show a warning when the PDF has a digital signature

entries.content:
Data structures such as arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, hash tables, trees, heaps, and graphs determine how a program stores data and how fast it can search, insert, and remove items. Big O notation describes how the number of steps grows as the input grows.

We just published a course on the freeCodeCamp.org YouTube channel that will teach you data structures and algorithms in Python, with every topic explained through custom animations and visualizations alongside Python code examples. This course is taught by Javid Bodurov.

The course is for beginners and only assumes the basics of Python: variables, loops, functions, and lists. You build each structure yourself, then compare it with tools Python already has, such as dict, set, deque, and heapq.

In this course, you will learn:

  • Big O, Arrays & Linked Lists

    How to measure how a program's steps grow, how data lives in memory, and why inserting at the head of a linked list changes only two pointers.
  • Stacks, Queues & Hash Tables

    How to solve the balanced brackets problem with a stack, use deque for fast queues, and handle collisions in a hash table.
  • Trees, Heaps & Graphs

    How binary search trees keep values ordered, how a heap gives you the smallest value first, and how breadth first search, depth first search, and Dijkstra's algorithm work on graphs.
  • Recursion, Searching & Sorting

    How memoization fixes a slow recursive Fibonacci, how binary search works on a sorted list, and how bubble, selection, insertion, merge, and quick sort compare.
  • Problem-Solving Patterns & Interview Problems

    How to recognize patterns such as two pointers and sliding windows, then bring everything together to approach coding interview problems.

Watch the full course on the freeCodeCamp.org YouTube channel (2.5-hour watch).

entries.content:
Therapy progress notes are written records of what happened during a therapy session. They may include what a client said, what the therapist observed, the topics discussed, and plans for the next session. Over time, these notes can add up to a large amount of text.

Reading one note helps us understand one session. But what if we want to look at several notes? Can we use text analysis to see how the language changes from one session to another?

Natural Language Processing (NLP) is a way of using computers to work with human language. With Python, you can break text into sentences, pick out language features, and use models to classify sentiment and emotion. In this tutorial, you’ll use spaCy’s language-processing pipeline for text processing and Hugging Face Transformers to run pretrained classification models.

You'll build a small NLP pipeline using fictional therapy notes. You’ll use spaCy to process the text, two ready-made Hugging Face models to classify sentiment and emotion, pandas to organize results by session, and Matplotlib to create charts.

You can find the complete project code in the GitHub repository.

We are not trying to decide whether therapy is working. The goal is to learn how to turn written text into data that we can review, question, and display in charts.

At the end, you'll have a practical Python project using spaCy, Hugging Face Transformers, pandas, and Matplotlib to explore sentiment, emotion, and language patterns in fictional therapy notes.

Note: This tutorial is for learning only and uses fictional text. The models have not been tested for clinical use. They cannot tell us whether therapy is working, identify problems in the therapist-client relationship, or replace a trained professional.

Table of Contents

What NLP Can and Cannot Tell Us

Natural Language Processing (NLP) is a part of artificial intelligence that helps computers work with human language. Common NLP tasks include breaking text into words and sentences, identifying grammar, finding names and places, and classifying sentiment and emotion.

Each task does something different. Tokenization breaks text into smaller pieces, such as words. Part-of-speech tagging identifies how a word is used in a sentence, such as a noun or verb. Lemmatization maps a word to its base form, while named-entity recognition identifies items such as people, organizations, and places. These are examples of the components available in spaCy’s processing pipelines. Sentiment analysis estimates whether text sounds positive or negative based on examples the model learned from. Emotion classification gives scores for emotion categories the model learned during training.

These results do not tell us what a person is really feeling. A therapy note may contain the therapist’s own observations, a client’s exact words, or the therapist’s summary of what the client said. A model may not know who said something or understand the full situation. In this tutorial, we’ll talk about model predictions and language patterns, not a person’s emotions or progress in therapy.

What We Are Building

Our project will analyze a small collection of fictional session notes and produce four types of results:

  • A sentiment prediction for each sentence
  • Emotion predictions for each sentence, along with average scores
  • Simple language features, such as counts of selected pronouns and phrases like “maybe” or “I think”
  • A timeline and dashboard to compare the results across sessions

The workflow is:

Figure 1. High-level view of the NLP workflow. The diagram also shows possible extensions, such as CSV and HTML reports, that are not implemented in every step of this tutorial.

We’ll keep the code in separate files so each part has one clear job. The project will not calculate a relationship-rupture score or label a clinical outcome.

Tools and Models

Python

Python will connect each part of the project. It also has many libraries for working with data and language.

spaCy is a Python library that helps us process text. Its processing pipeline can split text into tokens, assign part-of-speech tags, find base forms of words, and identify possible names or places. We’ll use its small English model, en_core_web_sm. This model works with general English, not specifically with therapy notes.

Hugging Face Transformers

We’ll use two pretrained classification models:

The first model, distilbert/distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english, classifies text as positive or negative. Its model card identifies it as a DistilBERT checkpoint fine-tuned on the Stanford Sentiment Treebank (SST-2), a dataset of general English sentences. DistilBERT itself is described in the research paper “DistilBERT, a distilled version of BERT: Smaller, faster, cheaper and lighter”. Neither the checkpoint nor the original DistilBERT paper establishes that this model is suitable for therapy notes.

The second model, j-hartmann/emotion-english-distilroberta-base, predicts seven categories: anger, disgust, fear, joy, neutral, sadness, and surprise. According to Jochen Hartmann’s model card, it was trained on a balanced collection drawn from six datasets, including social media posts, student self-reports, and dialogue. It has not been validated for analysing therapy progress notes.

These models help us learn how text classification works. But because they were trained on general text, we cannot assume they will work well on therapy notes.

pandas and Matplotlib

pandas will help us organize the results in a table called a DataFrame. Matplotlib will help us turn the results into charts.

pytest

pytest is a tool for checking that our code works as expected. We’ll use sample model results in some tests, so we can test the code without downloading the large model files.

Set Up the Python Project

Create a folder for the project, then move into it:

mkdir therapy_notes_nlp
cd therapy_notes_nlp
mkdir data src tests images

Your project folders and files should look like this:

therapy_notes_nlp/
├── data/
│   └── synthetic_notes.json
├── images/
├── src/
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── preprocessor.py
│   ├── sentiment.py
│   ├── emotions.py
│   ├── tracker.py
│   └── visualizer.py
├── tests/
│   ├── conftest.py
│   ├── test_analyzer.py
│   ├── test_emotions.py
│   ├── test_preprocessor.py
│   ├── test_sentiment.py
│   └── test_tracker.py
├── analyzer.py
├── main.py
├── pytest.ini
└── requirements.txt

Create a virtual environment and activate it. A virtual environment keeps this project’s Python packages separate from packages used by your other projects:

python -m venv .venv

# Windows
.venv\Scripts\activate

# macOS or Linux
source .venv/bin/activate

Add the following packages to 

requirements.txt
:
spacy>=3.8,<4.0
transformers>=4.45,<6.0
torch>=2.2
pandas>=2.2,<3.0
matplotlib>=3.8,<4.0
pytest>=8.0,<10.0

Install the packages and download spaCy’s English language model:

pip install -r requirements.txt
python -m spacy download en_core_web_sm

The first time you run the project, Hugging Face will download the model files. You can run the models on a CPU, but they may take longer than they would on a GPU.

Create a Synthetic Dataset

Therapy notes can contain private information. To protect people’s privacy, we’ll use made-up examples throughout this tutorial. This also means anyone can follow the project without the need to access real patient records.

Keep using fictional data for this tutorial. Do not replace it with real therapy notes unless you have the proper permission and safeguards, and have checked the laws and rules that apply to you.

spaCy can sometimes find names and other details in text, but it can also miss them. Removing a person’s name does not make a therapy note anonymous. For this tutorial, use only the fictional examples. Any real research project would need the right approval and privacy protections.

If you haven't already, create a file named 

synthetic_notes.json
in the 
data
folder:
[
  {
    "session": 1,
    "client_id": "SYNTHETIC_001",
    "note": "The fictional client described feeling overwhelmed by work demands. They said sleep had been difficult and they were unsure where to begin."
  },
  {
    "session": 2,
    "client_id": "SYNTHETIC_001",
    "note": "The fictional client discussed trying a new evening routine. They described one helpful moment but also mentioned ongoing worry."
  },
  {
    "session": 3,
    "client_id": "SYNTHETIC_001",
    "note": "The fictional client reported a stressful week and said they felt frustrated. They also identified one situation they handled differently."
  },
  {
    "session": 4,
    "client_id": "SYNTHETIC_001",
    "note": "The fictional client described feeling more hopeful about a work conversation. They remained concerned about maintaining the changes."
  },
  {
    "session": 5,
    "client_id": "SYNTHETIC_001",
    "note": "The fictional client questioned whether the current approach was useful and said they had expected a different pace. They wanted to discuss this concern."
  },
  {
    "session": 6,
    "client_id": "SYNTHETIC_001",
    "note": "The fictional client and therapist discussed the concern raised previously. The client described feeling heard, while noting that some questions remained unresolved."
  },
  {
    "session": 7,
    "client_id": "SYNTHETIC_001",
    "note": "The fictional client reflected on using a coping strategy during a difficult conversation. They described both relief and lingering nervousness."
  },
  {
    "session": 8,
    "client_id": "SYNTHETIC_001",
    "note": "The fictional client reviewed topics from the earlier sessions. They described changes they had noticed and identified challenges they still wanted to work on."
  }
]

Each item contains a session number, a made-up client ID, and a note. The examples include both positive and difficult experiences. We have not written them to force the models to give certain answers. We’ll run the models and examine the results they produce.

Preprocess Notes with spaCy

Before we classify the text, we’ll use spaCy to split each note into sentences and collect some basic information about the words.

In 

src/preprocessor.py:
from __future__ import annotations
from typing import Any
import spacy

MODEL_NAME = "en_core_web_sm"

def load_nlp(model_name: str = MODEL_NAME):
    return spacy.load(model_name)

_nlp = None

def get_nlp():
    global _nlp
    if _nlp is None:
        _nlp = load_nlp()
    return _nlp

def preprocess_note(text: str, nlp=None) -> dict[str, Any]:
    if not isinstance(text, str):
        raise TypeError("text must be a string")
    if not text.strip():
        return {
            "tokens": [], "lemmas": [], "sentences": [],
            "pos_tags": [], "entities": [],
            "token_count": 0, "sentence_count": 0
        }

    doc = (nlp or get_nlp())(text)
    tokens = [t.text.lower() for t in doc if not t.is_punct and not t.is_space]
    lemmas = [
        t.lemma_.lower() for t in doc
        if not t.is_stop and not t.is_punct and not t.is_space and t.is_alpha
    ]
    sentences = [s.text.strip() for s in doc.sents if s.text.strip()]
    pos_tags = [
        {"text": t.text, "pos": t.pos_, "tag": t.tag_}
        for t in doc if not t.is_punct and not t.is_space
    ]
    entities = [{"text": e.text, "label": e.label_} for e in doc.ents]

    return {
        "tokens": tokens,
        "lemmas": lemmas,
        "sentences": sentences,
        "pos_tags": pos_tags,
        "entities": entities,
        "token_count": len(tokens),
        "sentence_count": len(sentences)
    }

The 

_nlp = None
/ 
get_nlp()
pattern is worth pausing on. Loading a spaCy model takes a second or two, and you do not want that cost on every function call. By keeping 
_nlp
as a module-level variable, the model loads once, and every call after that reuses it. The 
(nlp or get_nlp())(text)
line might look odd at first, but it just means: use the model I was handed, or fall back to the default. This also makes the function easier to test later, since you can pass in a lightweight fake model instead of the real one.

One thing to notice: we pass the original sentences to the classifiers, not the cleaned tokens or lemmas. That is intentional. Words like "not" change a sentence's meaning, and stripping them before classification could quietly change what the model sees.

The entities field stores possible names, places, and other named items found by spaCy. It does not remove personal information or make the text anonymous.

Run Sentiment Analysis with DistilBERT

Sentiment analysis is a way to estimate whether text is more positive or negative based on examples a model learned from. The DistilBERT model we selected was trained further on SST-2, a general dataset of English sentences. It returns a positive score and a negative score for each sentence.

In 

src/sentiment.py
:
MODEL_ID = "distilbert/distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english"
_pipeline = None

def get_pipeline():
    global _pipeline
    if _pipeline is None:
        from transformers import pipeline
        _pipeline = pipeline(
            "text-classification", model=MODEL_ID, top_k=None
        )
    return _pipeline

def _normalise_prediction(prediction):
    if isinstance(prediction, dict):
        return [prediction]
    if prediction and isinstance(prediction[0], list):
        return prediction[0]
    return prediction

def analyze_sentiment(sentences: list[str], classifier=None) -> dict:
    clean = [s.strip() for s in sentences if isinstance(s, str) and s.strip()]
    if not clean:
        return {
            "sentence_results": [], "aggregate_score": None,
            "aggregate_label": None, "positive_ratio": 0.0,
            "negative_ratio": 0.0
        }

    model = classifier or get_pipeline()
    predictions = model(clean, truncation=True, batch_size=8)
    results = []

    for sentence, prediction in zip(clean, predictions):
        scores = _normalise_prediction(prediction)
        by_label = {
            item["label"].upper(): float(item["score"])
            for item in scores
        }
        positive = by_label.get("POSITIVE", 0.0)
        negative = by_label.get("NEGATIVE", 0.0)
        signed_score = positive - negative
        label = (
            "POSITIVE" if signed_score > 0
            else "NEGATIVE" if signed_score < 0
            else "BALANCED"
        )
        results.append({
            "sentence": sentence,
            "label": label,
            "positive_score": positive,
            "negative_score": negative,
            "signed_score": round(signed_score, 4)
        })

    values = [item["signed_score"] for item in results]
    aggregate = sum(values) / len(values)
    return {
        "sentence_results": results,
        "aggregate_score": round(aggregate, 4),
        "aggregate_label": (
            "POSITIVE" if aggregate > 0
            else "NEGATIVE" if aggregate < 0
            else "BALANCED"
        ),
        "positive_ratio": round(
            sum(item["label"] == "POSITIVE" for item in results) / len(results), 3
        ),
        "negative_ratio": round(
            sum(item["label"] == "NEGATIVE" for item in results) / len(results), 3
        )
    }


get_pipeline()
follows the same lazy-loading pattern as 
get_nlp()
: the model loads once and is reused on every subsequent call. Setting 
top_k=None
tells the Hugging Face pipeline to return scores for every label, not just the highest one. Without it, we would only get the winning label and could not compare both scores. 
truncation=True
cuts any input longer than 512 tokens, which is the maximum the model can process. 
batch_size=8
sends up to eight sentences to the model at once, which is faster than sending them one at a time.

_normalise_prediction()
exists because the pipeline can return results in different shapes depending on the version and configuration. It converts every shape into a consistent list of 
{"label": ..., "score": ...}
dictionaries so the rest of the function always has the same format to work with.

For each sentence, 

by_label
is a dictionary built from a comprehension that maps each uppercase label to its score. 
signed_score
subtracts the negative score from the positive score, giving a value between -1 and +1. At the end, the function averages all signed scores to produce one 
aggregate_score
for the session.

This index is simply a summary we created from the model's scores. It is not a medically approved measurement, a recovery score, or a measure of wellbeing. A score close to zero may also mean that positive and negative results balance each other out.

Classify Emotions with DistilRoBERTa

Sentiment and emotion classification are not the same. Sentiment gives a broad positive or negative result. Emotion classification looks at categories such as joy, sadness, anger, and fear.

In 

src/emotions.py
:
MODEL_ID = "j-hartmann/emotion-english-distilroberta-base"
_pipeline = None

def get_pipeline():
    global _pipeline
    if _pipeline is None:
        from transformers import pipeline
        _pipeline = pipeline(
            "text-classification", model=MODEL_ID, top_k=None
        )
    return _pipeline

def _normalise_prediction(prediction):
    if isinstance(prediction, dict):
        return [prediction]
    if prediction and isinstance(prediction[0], list):
        return prediction[0]
    return prediction

def detect_emotions(sentences: list[str], classifier=None) -> dict:
    clean = [s.strip() for s in sentences if isinstance(s, str) and s.strip()]
    if not clean:
        return {
            "per_sentence": [], "emotion_distribution": {},
            "session_dominant_emotion": None
        }

    model = classifier or get_pipeline()
    predictions = model(clean, truncation=True, batch_size=8)
    per_sentence = []
    totals = {}

    for sentence, prediction in zip(clean, predictions):
        scores = _normalise_prediction(prediction)
        score_map = {
            item["label"].lower(): float(item["score"])
            for item in scores
        }
        for label, score in score_map.items():
            totals[label] = totals.get(label, 0.0) + score
        dominant = max(score_map, key=score_map.get)
        per_sentence.append({
            "sentence": sentence,
            "dominant_emotion": dominant,
            "scores": score_map
        })

    distribution = {
        label: round(score / len(clean), 4)
        for label, score in totals.items()
    }
    dominant_session = max(distribution, key=distribution.get)
    return {
        "per_sentence": per_sentence,
        "emotion_distribution": distribution,
        "session_dominant_emotion": dominant_session
    }

The 

totals
dictionary accumulates scores across sentences. For each sentence, the loop adds the score for every emotion label to the running total. Using 
totals.get(label, 0.0)
safely handles the first time a label appears, starting it at zero rather than causing a key error.

max(score_map, key=score_map.get)
finds the label with the highest score in 
score_map
for that sentence. The 
key
argument tells 
max()
to compare values in the dictionary rather than the keys themselves.

After processing all sentences, 

distribution
divides each accumulated total by the number of sentences, giving a mean score per emotion across the whole session. 
max(distribution, key=distribution.get)
applies the same pattern to find the session-level dominant emotion.

These results are the model's predictions. They do not confirm how anyone feels. The model was trained on general English text, while therapy notes are written for a different purpose and may use different language. We should not assume that the model will work reliably on them.

Explore Linguistic Features

We can also count simple language features. For example, we can count how often first-person pronouns appear and look for phrases such as “maybe”, “perhaps”, and “I guess”. These are examples of hedging phrases, which people sometimes use when they are unsure or speaking cautiously.

Add this function to 

src/preprocessor.py
:
def extract_linguistic_features(text: str) -> dict:
    doc = get_nlp()(text)
    first_person = {
        "i", "me", "my", "mine", "myself", "we", "us",
        "our", "ours", "ourselves"
    }
    third_person = {
        "he", "him", "his", "himself", "she", "her", "hers",
        "herself", "they", "them", "their", "theirs",
        "themselves", "it", "its", "itself"
    }
    second_person = {"you", "your", "yours", "yourself", "yourselves"}

    pronouns = [token.text.lower() for token in doc if token.pos_ == "PRON"]
    first = sum(word in first_person for word in pronouns)
    third = sum(word in third_person for word in pronouns)
    second = sum(word in second_person for word in pronouns)
    total = first + third + second

    hedging_phrases = (
        "maybe", "perhaps", "possibly", "i guess", "not sure",
        "sort of", "kind of", "i think", "might"
    )
    lower = text.lower()
    hedging_count = sum(lower.count(phrase) for phrase in hedging_phrases)

    return {
        "first_person_count": first,
        "third_person_count": third,
        "second_person_count": second,
        "pronoun_count": total,
        "first_person_ratio": round(first / total, 3) if total else 0.0,
        "hedging_phrase_count": hedging_count
    }


token.pos_ == "PRON"
filters tokens by their part-of-speech tag. spaCy assigns this tag to words it identifies as pronouns. The three sets 
first_person
, 
third_person
, and 
second_person
define which lowercase words belong to each group. The generator expression inside 
sum()
checks whether each pronoun token's text belongs to that set and counts how many match.

first_person_ratio
divides the first-person count by the total pronoun count. The 
if total else 0.0
guard prevents a division-by-zero error when no pronouns appear in the text.

For hedging phrases, 

text.lower()
converts the whole note to lowercase before searching, so "Maybe" and "maybe" are treated the same. 
lower.count(phrase)
returns the number of times that phrase appears as a substring. The result for each phrase is added to 
hedging_count
.

These numbers are only counts. They do not explain why someone used a particular word or phrase. Their meaning depends on the context and the person who wrote the note. To understand whether these features are useful, we would need to compare them with carefully labelled examples. That is outside the scope of this tutorial.

Compare Results Across Sessions

Each session produces a set of results. We’ll use pandas to place the results in a table, with one row for each session. This makes it easier to compare the results over time.

In 

src/tracker.py
:
import pandas as pd

def build_session_timeline(session_results: list[dict]) -> pd.DataFrame:
    rows = []
    for result in session_results:
        sentiment = result["sentiment"]
        emotions = result["emotions"]
        linguistic = result["linguistic_features"]
        rows.append({
            "session": result["session"],
            "sentiment_index": sentiment["aggregate_score"],
            "sentiment_label": sentiment["aggregate_label"],
            "dominant_emotion": emotions["session_dominant_emotion"],
            "first_person_ratio": linguistic["first_person_ratio"],
            "hedging_phrase_count": linguistic["hedging_phrase_count"],
            "sentence_count": result["sentence_count"]
        })

    columns = [
        "session", "sentiment_index", "sentiment_label",
        "dominant_emotion", "first_person_ratio",
        "hedging_phrase_count", "sentence_count"
    ]
    if not rows:
        return pd.DataFrame(columns=columns)
    return pd.DataFrame(rows).sort_values("session").reset_index(drop=True)

def describe_sentiment_shift(df: pd.DataFrame) -> dict:
    if df.empty:
        return {
            "session_count": 0,
            "first_half_mean": None,
            "second_half_mean": None,
            "difference": None,
            "description": "No sessions to compare"
        }

    midpoint = max(1, len(df) // 2)
    first = df.iloc[:midpoint]["sentiment_index"].dropna()
    second = df.iloc[midpoint:]["sentiment_index"].dropna()
    first_mean = float(first.mean()) if not first.empty else None
    second_mean = float(second.mean()) if not second.empty else None
    difference = (
        second_mean - first_mean
        if first_mean is not None and second_mean is not None
        else None
    )

    if difference is None:
        description = "Insufficient non-missing scores to compare halves"
    elif difference > 0.05:
        description = "Higher average model sentiment index in the second half"
    elif difference < -0.05:
        description = "Lower average model sentiment index in the second half"
    else:
        description = "Little difference between the two half-period averages"

    return {
        "session_count": len(df),
        "first_half_mean": first_mean,
        "second_half_mean": second_mean,
        "difference": round(difference, 4) if difference is not None else None,
        "description": description
    }


build_session_timeline()
loops through each session result, pulls the fields it needs from the nested dictionaries, and appends a flat dictionary as a row. 
pd.DataFrame(rows)
turns the list of rows into a table. 
.sort_values("session")
orders the rows by session number, and 
.reset_index(drop=True)
replaces the index with a clean sequence starting at zero.

In 

describe_sentiment_shift()
, 
df.iloc[:midpoint]
selects the first half of rows by position. 
.dropna()
removes any rows where 
sentiment_index
is missing before calculating the mean, so a single missing value does not make the whole average 
NaN
. The 0.05 threshold keeps the description from calling a very small numerical difference meaningful.

The description refers only to the model's sentiment index. We avoid labels such as "strong improvement" or "clinical deterioration" because a change in a model's score does not prove that someone's mental health or therapy progress has changed.

Visualize the Outputs

Charts can make results easier to understand than a table alone. We’ll create four charts: the sentiment index, the most likely emotion predicted for each session, the share of first-person pronouns, and the number of hedging phrases.

In 

src/visualizer.py
:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd

def plot_dashboard(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    output_path: str = "images/session_dashboard.png"
):
    if df.empty:
        raise ValueError("Cannot plot an empty session timeline")

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12, 8))
    sessions = df["session"]

    axes[0, 0].plot(sessions, df["sentiment_index"], marker="o")
    axes[0, 0].axhline(0, linestyle="--", linewidth=1)
    axes[0, 0].set(
        title="Model sentiment index by session",
        xlabel="Session",
        ylabel="Positive score minus negative score"
    )

    emotion_codes = {
        name: i for i, name in enumerate(
            sorted(df["dominant_emotion"].dropna().unique())
        )
    }
    emotion_values = [
        emotion_codes.get(value, -1)
        for value in df["dominant_emotion"]
    ]
    axes[0, 1].scatter(sessions, emotion_values)
    axes[0, 1].set(
        title="Dominant predicted emotion",
        xlabel="Session",
        ylabel="Emotion category"
    )
    axes[0, 1].set_yticks(
        list(emotion_codes.values()), list(emotion_codes.keys())
    )

    axes[1, 0].plot(sessions, df["first_person_ratio"], marker="o")
    axes[1, 0].set(
        title="First-person pronoun share",
        xlabel="Session",
        ylabel="Share of counted pronouns",
        ylim=(0, 1)
    )

    axes[1, 1].bar(sessions, df["hedging_phrase_count"])
    axes[1, 1].set(
        title="Selected hedging phrases",
        xlabel="Session",
        ylabel="Phrase count"
    )

    fig.suptitle("Exploratory text-analysis outputs (synthetic data)")
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(output_path, dpi=160, bbox_inches="tight")
    plt.close(fig)
    return output_path


plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12, 8))
creates a figure with a 2 by 2 grid of subplots. It returns the figure object 
fig
and a 2D array 
axes
where 
axes[row, col]
gives each chart.

The sentiment chart uses 

axes[0, 0].axhline(0)
to draw a horizontal reference line at zero. This makes it easy to see at a glance which sessions produced a net-positive or net-negative index.

The emotion chart needs an extra step because Matplotlib scatter plots require numbers, not strings. 

emotion_codes
is a dictionary that maps each unique emotion label to an integer using 
enumerate
. 
emotion_values
converts the dominant emotion column to those integers for plotting. 
set_yticks()
then restores the original label names on the y-axis, so the chart shows words instead of numbers.

fig.tight_layout()
automatically adjusts spacing between the subplots so titles and labels do not overlap. 
fig.savefig()
writes the finished figure to a file, and 
plt.close(fig)
releases the memory the figure used.

[Figure 2: figure-2.png]

Figure 2. Example dashboard from fictional sessions. The scores and language counts are model outputs and text features, not measures of therapy progress.

Each chart shows a different result. The sentiment chart shows the index we calculated from the model scores. The emotion chart shows the category with the highest score in each session. The other two charts show counts or proportions taken directly from the text.

This dashboard is not a report on someone’s progress in therapy. It only displays the results produced by our code and the models we selected.

Connect the Pipeline

Next, we’ll connect the different parts of the project using a Python class. This gives us one place to start when we want to analyse a single note or several notes.

In 

analyzer.py
:
from src.preprocessor import preprocess_note, extract_linguistic_features
from src.sentiment import analyze_sentiment
from src.emotions import detect_emotions
from src.tracker import build_session_timeline, describe_sentiment_shift

class TherapyNoteAnalyzer:
    def analyze_session(self, note_data: dict) -> dict:
        required = {"session", "client_id", "note"}
        missing = required - note_data.keys()
        if missing:
            raise ValueError(f"Missing required fields: {sorted(missing)}")

        processed = preprocess_note(note_data["note"])
        sentiment = analyze_sentiment(processed["sentences"])
        emotions = detect_emotions(processed["sentences"])
        linguistic = extract_linguistic_features(note_data["note"])

        return {
            "session": note_data["session"],
            "client_id": note_data["client_id"],
            "sentence_count": processed["sentence_count"],
            "sentiment": sentiment,
            "emotions": emotions,
            "linguistic_features": linguistic,
            "entity_candidates": processed["entities"]
        }

    def analyze_all(self, notes: list[dict]) -> dict:
        if not notes:
            timeline = build_session_timeline([])
            return {
                "client_id": None,
                "session_results": [],
                "timeline": timeline,
                "sentiment_comparison": describe_sentiment_shift(timeline)
            }

        client_ids = {item.get("client_id") for item in notes}
        if len(client_ids) != 1:
            raise ValueError(
                "This example expects notes for one synthetic client at a time"
            )

        results = [self.analyze_session(item) for item in notes]
        timeline = build_session_timeline(results)
        return {
            "client_id": next(iter(client_ids)),
            "session_results": results,
            "timeline": timeline,
            "sentiment_comparison": describe_sentiment_shift(timeline)
        }

Finally, in 

main.py
:
import json
from pathlib import Path
from analyzer import TherapyNoteAnalyzer
from src.visualizer import plot_dashboard

def main():
    with Path("data/synthetic_notes.json").open(encoding="utf-8") as file:
        notes = json.load(file)

    results = TherapyNoteAnalyzer().analyze_all(notes)
    print(results["timeline"].to_string(index=False))
    print("\nDescriptive comparison:", results["sentiment_comparison"])

    output = plot_dashboard(results["timeline"])
    print(f"\nSaved dashboard to {output}")
    print("Reminder: these model outputs are exploratory, not clinical assessments.")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Run the project from its root directory:

python main.py

The first time you run the script, it will download both Hugging Face models. It will then print a table of the session results and save a dashboard image in the images folder.

The results may differ depending on the model version and how the code is run. Always check the results from your own run. Say what the model predicted, rather than saying what a session “showed” or “revealed”. A model prediction is not proof of what happened.

Test the Project

Testing helps us check whether our functions work with normal inputs and unusual cases, such as empty text. Passing these tests does not prove that a model is accurate or useful in a clinical setting.

For the sentiment and emotion tests, we’ll use fake classifiers that return results we choose in advance. This keeps the tests quick and means we do not need to download the model files.

A simplified sentiment test looks like this:

from src.sentiment import analyze_sentiment

class FakeSentiment:
    def __call__(self, texts, **kwargs):
        return [
            [
                {"label": "POSITIVE", "score": 0.8},
                {"label": "NEGATIVE", "score": 0.2}
            ],
            [
                {"label": "POSITIVE", "score": 0.1},
                {"label": "NEGATIVE", "score": 0.9}
            ]
        ][:len(texts)]

def test_sentiment_score_is_positive_minus_negative():
    result = analyze_sentiment(
        ["Good sentence.", "Bad sentence."],
        classifier=FakeSentiment()
    )
    assert result["sentence_results"][0]["signed_score"] == 0.6
    assert result["sentence_results"][1]["signed_score"] == -0.8


FakeSentiment
works as a drop-in replacement for the real model because it defines 
__call__
. When Python sees 
model(clean, ...)
, it calls 
model.__call__(clean, ...)
, so any object with that method behaves like a callable. 
FakeSentiment.__call__
returns a fixed list of scores regardless of the input text, which means the test checks the calculation logic without downloading the model.

[:len(texts)]
slices the return value to match the number of input sentences. This prevents the fake classifier from returning more results than there are inputs, which would cause the 
zip()
in 
analyze_sentiment
to behave unexpectedly.

Passing 

classifier=FakeSentiment()
to 
analyze_sentiment
overrides 
get_pipeline()
for that call. This pattern is called dependency injection: the function accepts its dependency from outside rather than creating it internally, which makes the function easier to test and reuse.

The full project includes tests for empty inputs, sentence splitting, word handling, sentiment score calculations, emotion score summaries, sorting sessions, empty timelines, and checking that required input fields are present.

Run the test suite from the project root:

python -m pytest -q

The project archive contains 15 tests, and all 15 passed when the project was checked. Some tests use made-up model results, while others use a small spaCy setup to check selected text-processing steps. These tests do not measure model accuracy, confirm that the emotion labels are correct, or show how the models perform on real therapy notes.

Limitations and Ethical Considerations

Because this project uses therapy-related text, we need to think carefully about privacy, the limits of the models, and the difference between language patterns and a professional clinical assessment.

General-domain models are not clinical models

The DistilBERT model was trained on SST-2, not on therapy notes. The DistilRoBERTa model was trained on a mix of general English text. We do not know how well either model works on clinical notes unless it is tested separately using suitable data and clear labels. The models may also handle formal writing, writing by people who speak English as an additional language, and different cultural ways of expressing distress poorly. Their training data was not designed to cover all these situations.

Sentiment is not therapeutic progress

A positive sentence does not prove that a client is getting better. A negative sentence does not prove that therapy is failing. A note may contain the therapist’s view, the client’s own words, a difficult event, or a mix of these. The model may not be able to tell the difference.

Linguistic features are not psychological diagnoses

Pronoun counts and hedging phrases are simple features found in the text. A change in these counts does not prove that a client is withdrawing, avoiding a topic, losing trust, or having a problem with the therapist. We removed the rupture score from an earlier version of this project because its scoring rules and alert level had not been tested or approved for clinical use.

Privacy requirements depend on jurisdiction

In the United States, HIPAA applies to certain healthcare organisations and their business partners. Other countries have their own data protection and healthcare privacy laws. Before using real records, an organisation must check the laws that apply, its own policies, the legal reason for using the data, any required consent, the services and vendors involved, security measures, and how long the data will be kept. This tutorial is not a substitute for that review. Even if HIPAA does not apply where you live, that does not mean it is safe or ethical to process real therapy notes.

Human oversight and transparency

This project is not made for clinical decisions, and it should not be used as the basis for them. Any NLP tool considered for real healthcare work would need to be tested for that specific setting. It would also need privacy and bias reviews, clear documentation, and oversight from qualified professionals. People whose information is used should be told about it as required by the relevant rules.

Conclusion and Further Learning

In this project, we built an NLP workflow with spaCy, Hugging Face Transformers, pandas, and Matplotlib. Using fictional therapy notes, we showed how to split text into sentences, classify sentiment and emotion, count language features, compare sessions, create charts, and test the code.

NLP can help turn large amounts of written text into data that we can organise and explore. But the results have limits, especially when we use a general-purpose model on a sensitive type of text it was not trained or tested to understand.

If you want to build on this project, here are a few ideas:

Try different sentiment models and compare their predictions. Note where they agree and where they differ.

Before making claims about model performance, create a dataset with human-checked labels and get the proper ethical approval to use it.

If you have correct labels to compare against, use measures such as precision, recall, F1-score, and a confusion matrix to check the model’s results.

Explore clinical NLP tools such as scispaCy. Remember that tools designed for medical text still need to be tested for the task you want to use them for.

Build a Streamlit app that lets people try the project with fictional examples only.

To learn more, read the spaCy documentation, the DistilBERT sentiment model card, and the DistilRoBERTa emotion model card. You can also read Edward S. Bordin’s 1979 paper, “The Generalizability of the Psychoanalytic Concept of the Working Alliance”, for background on the working relationship between a therapist and client.

NLP can help us study large amounts of text. But using it responsibly means understanding the data, knowing what a model was trained to do, and being clear about what its results cannot tell us.

If you'd like to explore the project further, you can check out the GitHub repository. I've included the code and project structure there, so you can see how everything works. It's also a good starting point if you're curious about how Python and NLP apply to areas like healthcare, health tech, clinical NLP, and AI. There's still a lot to explore in this space, and I hope the project gives you a few ideas to build on.

entries.title: How to Build a Translator with Chrome’s Built-In AI
entries.summary: Most translation features work the same way. The user types text, your app sends it to a translation API, and the API sends a translation back. That works, but every request adds cost and latency, and
entries.content:
Most translation features work the same way. The user types text, your app sends it to a translation API, and the API sends a translation back. That works, but every request adds cost and latency, and your users' text leaves their device.

Chrome now ships two built-in AI APIs that change this: the Translator API and the Language Detector API. Chrome downloads small, specialized models on demand and runs them on the user's device. You don't host a model, run an inference server, or pay per request. You call a JavaScript API.

In this tutorial, you'll build a translator in Next.js that:

  • Detects the language of the text a user types.
  • Translates it into a language they choose.
  • Streams the translation into the page as Chrome produces it.
  • Shows language-pack download progress, and lets the user cancel.
  • Copies the translation, reads it aloud, and swaps the two languages.
  • Handles browsers that don't support the APIs.

Table of Contents

Prerequisites

You should be comfortable with:

  • JavaScript or TypeScript
  • React basics (components, props, 
    useState
    , 
    useEffect
    )
  • Running commands in a terminal

You'll need:

  • Node.js 20.9 or later.
  • Desktop Chrome 138 or later. The Translator and Language Detector APIs work in Chrome on desktop. They don't work on mobile devices, and Firefox and Safari don't support them. Chrome's browser-support table also lists Edge (148). I tested this tutorial in Chrome 156 on macOS.

You don't need to know anything about machine learning.

Internationalization vs AI Translation

Before you write code, separate two ideas that are easy to confuse.

Internationalization (i18n) prepares your interface for multiple languages and regions: language selection, locale-aware dates, numbers and currencies, right-to-left (RTL) layout, and static interface strings that a person wrote and reviewed:

const messages = {
  en: { welcome: "Welcome", description: "Explore our platform" },
  fr: { welcome: "Bienvenue", description: "Explorez notre plateforme" },
  es: { welcome: "Bienvenido", description: "Explora nuestra plataforma" },
};

AI-powered translation generates translations on the fly for content nobody wrote ahead of time, such as comments, reviews, support messages and posts.

Traditional i18nAI-powered translation
Uses predefined translationsGenerates translations dynamically
Ideal for interface textIdeal for user-generated content
Usually developer-managedCan process arbitrary text
Predictable outputOutput may vary

AI translation complements i18n. It doesn't replace it. You still need curated strings for buttons and menus. The Translator API fills the gap for everything else.

Chrome's documentation gives a good example: in a support chat, users write in their first language, and your site translates the message into your agent's language before the message leaves the user's device.

How Chrome's Built-In AI APIs Work

There are two APIs, and they work together:

  • LanguageDetector
    takes text and returns a ranked list of languages, each with a confidence score between 0 and 1.
  • Translator
    is created for one language pair, such as English to Spanish, and translates text between them.

Here's what makes them different from calling a cloud API, or from running a model yourself with a library such as Transformers.js:

  • The browser owns the model. You don't bundle or host model files. Chrome downloads them the first time a site needs them.
  • Translation uses language packs. Chrome's docs describe a language pack as "like a dictionary for a given language", downloaded on demand. The first translation for a pair triggers a download, and later ones reuse it.
  • Everything is asynchronous and permission-aware. You check 
    availability()
    first, then call 
    create()
    , and you can watch download progress.

There are four constraints you need to design around, all from Chrome's documentation:

  • User activation. Creating a translator or detector needs a user gesture, such as a click, when a model has to be downloaded.
  • Not in Web Workers. Neither API is available in workers, so you call them from the main thread. (The calls are asynchronous and the model runs outside your JavaScript thread, so this doesn't block your UI.)
  • Sequential processing. Translations are processed one after another. A large request blocks later ones, so chunk work and show a loading indicator.
  • Top-level windows only. By default, the APIs work in top-level windows and same-origin iframes. Cross-origin iframes need a Permissions Policy 
    allow
    attribute.

The 

availability()
method for both APIs returns one of four values, and your UI should handle each:
ValueMeaning
unavailable
 The browser doesn't support these options.
downloadable
 Supported, but a model must be downloaded first.
downloading
 Supported, and a download is already in progress.
available
 Supported and ready to use with no download.

One privacy detail: Chrome hides the download status of specific language pairs to protect user privacy. Until your site creates a translator for a pair, all pairs are reported as 

downloadable
.

Try the APIs in the Playground First

Before you write code, experiment. The Built-in AI Playground presents the AI features Chrome exposes as JavaScript APIs, including both of these. Open it in desktop Chrome and try this:

  • Paste a few sentences in different languages into the language detector, and read the confidence scores.
  • Try a single word, then a full sentence. Chrome's documentation warns that short input gives low-accuracy results, so compare the confidence values.
  • Translate between a couple of language pairs. The first translation for a pair may pause while Chrome downloads a language pack.

You'll build exactly this behaviour into the app.

How to Set Up the Next.js Project

Create a Next.js app with TypeScript and the App Router. Answer the remaining prompts however you like:

npx create-next-app@latest chrome-ai-translator --ts --app --no-tailwind --no-src-dir --import-alias "@/*"
cd chrome-ai-translator

Then install the TypeScript definitions for Chrome's built-in AI APIs. TypeScript doesn't know about 

Translator
or 
LanguageDetector
yet, because they aren't in the standard DOM types:
npm install -D @types/dom-chromium-ai

The package declares 

Translator
, 
LanguageDetector
and the related types globally, so you don't import anything. Your editor will now autocomplete 
Translator.create()
and flag mistakes.

Delete 

app/page.module.css
and the unused images in 
public/
. You'll replace 
app/page.tsx
, 
app/layout.tsx
and 
app/globals.css
. Create these folders next to 
app/
:
chrome-ai-translator/
├── app/
│   ├── globals.css
│   ├── layout.tsx
│   └── page.tsx
├── components/
│   ├── language-select.tsx
│   ├── text-panel.tsx
│   ├── translator-app.tsx
│   └── unsupported-notice.tsx
├── hooks/
│   └── use-translation.ts
└── lib/
    ├── chrome-ai.ts
    └── languages.ts

Each folder has one job:

  • lib/
    contains plain TypeScript that talks to Chrome's APIs.
  • hooks/
    turns that into React state.
  • components/
    contains the UI.
  • app/
    contains the Next.js page and layout.

How to Define the Languages

Create 

lib/languages.ts
. It lists the languages Chrome's Translator API supports (from Chrome's documentation). The Translator API uses BCP 47 codes such as 
es
or 
zh-Hant
:
/** Sentinel value for "detect the source language for me". */
export const AUTO = "auto";

export interface Language {
  /** BCP 47 code, as expected by the Translator API. */
  code: string;
  name: string;
  rtl?: boolean;
}

export const LANGUAGES: Language[] = [
  { code: "ar", name: "Arabic", rtl: true },
  { code: "de", name: "German" },
  { code: "en", name: "English" },
  { code: "es", name: "Spanish" },
  { code: "fr", name: "French" },
  { code: "he", name: "Hebrew", rtl: true },
  // ...the full list of 39 languages is in the repository
  { code: "zh", name: "Chinese (Simplified)" },
  { code: "zh-Hant", name: "Chinese (Traditional)" },
];

export function languageName(code: string): string {
  return LANGUAGES.find((language) => language.code === code)?.name ?? code;
}

export function isRtl(code: string): boolean {
  return LANGUAGES.find((language) => language.code === code)?.rtl ?? false;
}

A hard-coded list is fine for a tutorial, but Chrome says the list is specific to its implementation and subject to change, and there's no function yet to retrieve it dynamically. That's why the app still calls 

Translator.availability()
before every translation. The list only decides what appears in the dropdowns.

The 

rtl
flag lets the output render right-to-left for Arabic and Hebrew.

How to Wrap the Chrome APIs

Now you'll create 

lib/chrome-ai.ts
. This file is the heart of the project. It holds every call to Chrome's Translator and Language Detector APIs, so the rest of the app never touches them directly.

You'll build it one piece at a time and add each piece below the previous one. Everything in this file runs in the browser only, so you'll import it from Client Components.

Step 1: Add the shared constants, types and errors

Start the file with a few small definitions that the later functions depend on:

/**
 * Thin helpers around Chrome's built-in Translator and Language Detector APIs.
 * Everything here runs in the browser only. Import it from Client Components.
 */

/** Below this confidence we ask the user to pick the language instead of guessing. */
export const CONFIDENCE_THRESHOLD = 0.6;

export type DownloadProgress = (fraction: number) => void;

export class LowConfidenceError extends Error {
  constructor() {
    super("We couldn't tell which language this is. Choose the source language manually.");
  }
}

export class UnsupportedPairError extends Error {
  constructor(source: string, target: string) {
    super(`Chrome can't translate from "${source}" to "${target}" on this device.`);
  }
}

Here's what each piece does:

  • CONFIDENCE_THRESHOLD
    is the minimum confidence score we accept from the language detector. Detection is a probability, not a fact. Chrome's docs warn that very short phrases and single words give low-accuracy results, and recommend treating the result as unknown when confidence is too low. The hook you'll write later compares each result to this number. 
    0.6
    is a starting point you can tune for your own users.
  • DownloadProgress
    is the type of the callback that receives download progress. Chrome reports progress as a fraction from 
    0
    to 
    1
    , so 
    0.5
    means half of the language pack has downloaded.
  • LowConfidenceError
    is thrown when the detector can't tell what language the text is in. Giving it its own class lets the hook tell it apart from other failures, and its message tells the user what to do next.
  • UnsupportedPairError
    is thrown when Chrome says it can't translate between two languages. It includes both language codes, so the user knows which pair failed.

Step 2: Check whether the browser supports the APIs

Add the feature-detection function:

/** Feature detection. Always false on the server, where `self.Translator` doesn't exist. */
export function isBuiltInAISupported(): boolean {
  return typeof self !== "undefined" && "Translator" in self && "LanguageDetector" in self;
}

Next.js renders your components on the server first, and on the server there is no 

self.Translator
. This function checks three things:
  • typeof self !== "undefined"
    makes sure we're in a context where 
    self
    exists at all, so the function can't crash on the server.
  • "Translator" in self
    is the check Chrome's documentation recommends for the Translator API.
  • "LanguageDetector" in self
    is the matching check for the Language Detector API. The app needs both, so it only reports support when both exist.

The function returns 

true
or 
false
and never throws. You'll use it later to decide whether to show the translator or a "not supported" notice.

Step 3: Create the language detector

Next, add the code that creates the detector. This is the first place you'll see the 

monitor
callback and download progress:
let detectorPromise: Promise | null = null;

function getDetector(onProgress?: DownloadProgress) {
  detectorPromise ??= LanguageDetector.create({
    monitor(monitor) {
      monitor.addEventListener("downloadprogress", (event) => onProgress?.(event.loaded));
    },
  });
  // If creation fails (e.g. no user activation), allow a retry on the next click.
  detectorPromise.catch(() => {
    detectorPromise = null;
  });
  return detectorPromise;
}

Here's how 

getDetector()
works:
  • detectorPromise
    is a module-level variable that holds the detector. We store the promise, not the finished detector. That way, if two parts of the app ask for a detector at the same moment, they share one creation instead of starting two.
  • ??=
    means "assign only if the variable is 
    null
    or 
    undefined
    ". The first call runs 
    LanguageDetector.create()
    , and every later call reuses the stored promise.
  • The 
    monitor
    option is a callback that Chrome calls with a 
    CreateMonitor
    object. We listen for its 
    downloadprogress
    event and pass 
    event.loaded
    , the 0-to-1 fraction, to 
    onProgress
    . Chrome's detection model is small and may already be on the device, so this event might never fire. We still handle it, because it can fire the first time.
  • The 
    .catch()
    resets 
    detectorPromise
    to 
    null
    if creation fails. Without it, a failed attempt (for example, when Chrome needs a user click that it didn't get) would be cached forever, and the user could never retry.

Step 4: Detect the language of some text

Now add the function that uses the detector:

export interface Detection {
  language: string;
  confidence: number;
}

export async function detectLanguage(
  text: string,
  onProgress?: DownloadProgress,
  signal?: AbortSignal,
): Promise {
  const detector = await getDetector(onProgress);
  // Results are ranked from most to least likely. The last entry is always "und" (undetermined).
  const [top] = await detector.detect(text, { signal });
  if (!top?.detectedLanguage || top.detectedLanguage === "und") return null;
  return { language: top.detectedLanguage, confidence: top.confidence ?? 0 };
}

This is what the code does:

  • The 
    Detection
    interface describes what we return: a BCP 47 language code such as 
    "es"
    , and a confidence score between 
    0
    and 
    1
    .
  • detectLanguage()
    first waits for the detector from 
    getDetector()
    . It passes 
    onProgress
    along so the UI can show a download bar.
  • detector.detect(text, { signal })
    returns a list of guesses ranked from most to least likely, each with a 
    detectedLanguage
    and a 
    confidence
    . The 
    signal
    is an 
    AbortSignal
    , so the user can cancel a detection in progress.
  • The array destructuring 
    [top]
    takes only the best guess.
  • The last item in Chrome's results is always 
    und
    , which means "undetermined". It's the probability that the text isn't in a language the model knows. If the best guess is missing or is 
    und
    , the function returns 
    null
    , which means "no answer".
  • Otherwise, it returns the language and confidence. The 
    ?? 0
    is a safety net, because TypeScript types 
    confidence
    as optional.

Step 5: Create and cache translators

Translation is where the language-pair logic lives. Add this next:

// A Translator is tied to one language pair. Creating one is expensive, so we keep them around.
const translators = new Map();

export async function getTranslator(
  sourceLanguage: string,
  targetLanguage: string,
  onProgress?: DownloadProgress,
  signal?: AbortSignal,
): Promise {
  const key = `${sourceLanguage}>${targetLanguage}`;
  const cached = translators.get(key);
  if (cached) return cached;

  const availability = await Translator.availability({ sourceLanguage, targetLanguage });
  if (availability === "unavailable") {
    throw new UnsupportedPairError(sourceLanguage, targetLanguage);
  }

  const translator = await Translator.create({
    sourceLanguage,
    targetLanguage,
    signal,
    monitor(monitor) {
      monitor.addEventListener("downloadprogress", (event) => onProgress?.(event.loaded));
    },
  });
  translators.set(key, translator);
  return translator;
}

This function follows the lifecycle described in Chrome's documentation, in four stages:

  • Check the cache. A 
    Translator
    is tied to exactly one language pair. Creating one is expensive, so we keep a 
    Map
    of them, keyed by a string like 
    "en>es"
    . If we already have a translator for this pair, we return it immediately. That's why translating a second sentence is fast.
  • Check availability. 
    Translator.availability()
    tells us whether Chrome can handle this pair. It returns 
    unavailable
    , 
    downloadable
    , 
    downloading
    or 
    available
    . If it's 
    unavailable
    , we throw 
    UnsupportedPairError
    before attempting anything else, so no download starts for a pair that can never work.
  • Create the translator. 
    Translator.create()
    receives the language pair, the 
    signal
    for cancellation, and a 
    monitor
    that reports download progress exactly like the detector did. If a language pack has to be downloaded, Chrome starts the download automatically here. This is also the step that needs a user gesture, such as a click, when a download is required.
  • Store and return. We save the new translator in the 
    Map
    for next time and return it.

Step 6: Release the models when you're done

Add a function that frees memory:

/** Releases the memory held by the models. Call it when the user leaves the feature. */
export async function destroyAll() {
  for (const translator of translators.values()) translator.destroy();
  translators.clear();
  const pending = detectorPromise;
  detectorPromise = null;
  (await pending?.catch(() => null))?.destroy();
}

MDN recommends calling 

destroy()
once you've finished with a 
Translator
or 
LanguageDetector
, because they can use a lot of resources. This function does that for everything we created:
  • The 
    for
    loop calls 
    destroy()
    on every cached translator, and 
    translators.clear()
    empties the cache so a later request creates a fresh one.
  • The detector is trickier, because we stored a promise rather than the detector itself. We copy the promise into 
    pending
    , reset the shared variable to 
    null
    , and then wait for the promise.
  • pending?.catch(() => null)
    handles two edge cases: there might be no detector at all, or creation might have failed. In both cases we get 
    null
    back, and the final 
    ?.destroy()
    does nothing.

The hook you'll write next calls 

destroyAll()
when the component unmounts.

Step 7: Turn API errors into helpful messages

Finally, add the function that explains failures to the user:

/** Turns the DOMExceptions these APIs throw into messages a user can act on. */
export function describeError(error: unknown): string {
  if (error instanceof DOMException) {
    switch (error.name) {
      case "NotAllowedError":
        return "Chrome needs a fresh click to start the download. Press Translate again.";
      case "NotSupportedError":
        // Also thrown on a brand-new Chrome profile while it is still fetching its components.
        return "Chrome couldn't prepare this translation. If this is your first use, wait a moment and try again. Otherwise, this language may not be supported on your device.";
      case "QuotaExceededError":
        return "That text is too long. Try translating a shorter passage.";
      case "NetworkError":
        return "The language pack couldn't be downloaded. Check your connection and try again.";
    }
  }
  return error instanceof Error ? error.message : "Something went wrong.";
}

The built-in AI APIs report problems by throwing a 

DOMException
, and the exception's 
name
says what went wrong. This function maps each name to a message a person can act on:
  • NotAllowedError
    : Chrome needed a user gesture, like a click, to start a download and didn't get one. Asking the user to press Translate again fixes it.
  • NotSupportedError
    : MDN documents this as the error thrown when the requested languages aren't supported. During testing I also saw it on a brand-new Chrome profile, on the very first attempt, while Chrome was still preparing its components. The next attempt worked. The message covers both cases.
  • QuotaExceededError
    : MDN documents this as the error thrown when the input is larger than the available quota. It means the text is too long.
  • NetworkError
    : the language pack couldn't be downloaded.

For anything else, the function falls back to the error's own message if it's a normal 

Error
, or to a generic message.

How to Build the Translation Hook

Create

"use client";

import { useCallback, useEffect, useRef, useState } from "react";
import { AUTO } from "@/lib/languages";
import {
  CONFIDENCE_THRESHOLD,
  LowConfidenceError,
  describeError,
  destroyAll,
  detectLanguage,
  getTranslator,
  type Detection,
} from "@/lib/chrome-ai";

export type Phase = "idle" | "detecting" | "preparing" | "translating";

export function useTranslation() {
  const [phase, setPhase] = useState("idle");
  const [downloadProgress, setDownloadProgress] = useState(null);
  const [output, setOutput] = useState("");
  const [detected, setDetected] = useState(null);
  const [error, setError] = useState(null);
  const controllerRef = useRef(null);

  // Free the models when the component unmounts.
  useEffect(() => {
    return () => {
      controllerRef.current?.abort();
      void destroyAll();
    };
  }, []);

  const translate = useCallback(async (text: string, source: string, target: string) => {
    controllerRef.current?.abort();
    const controller = new AbortController();
    controllerRef.current = controller;
    const { signal } = controller;

    setError(null);
    setOutput("");
    setDetected(null);
    setDownloadProgress(null);

    try {
      let from = source;

      if (source === AUTO) {
        setPhase("detecting");
        const result = await detectLanguage(text, setDownloadProgress, signal);
        if (!result || result.confidence < CONFIDENCE_THRESHOLD) throw new LowConfidenceError();
        setDetected(result);
        from = result.language;
      }

      if (from === target) {
        throw new Error("The source and target languages are the same.");
      }

      setPhase("preparing");
      setDownloadProgress(null);
      const translator = await getTranslator(from, target, setDownloadProgress, signal);

      setPhase("translating");
      setDownloadProgress(null);
      // Streaming shows text as soon as it's ready, which feels faster for longer input.
      const reader = translator.translateStreaming(text, { signal }).getReader();
      for (;;) {
        const { done, value } = await reader.read();
        if (done) break;
        setOutput((current) => current + value);
      }
    } catch (caught) {
      if (!signal.aborted) setError(describeError(caught));
    } finally {
      if (controllerRef.current === controller) {
        controllerRef.current = null;
        setPhase("idle");
        setDownloadProgress(null);
      }
    }
  }, []);

  const cancel = useCallback(() => controllerRef.current?.abort(), []);

  const reset = useCallback(() => {
    setOutput("");
    setDetected(null);
    setError(null);
  }, []);

  return { phase, downloadProgress, output, detected, error, translate, cancel, reset };
}

Here's what happens when the user clicks Translate:

  • Cancel anything in flight and create a new 
    AbortController
    . Its 
    signal
    goes into every call, so one 
    cancel()
    stops detection, downloading and translating.
  • Detect, if needed. When the source is "Detect language", we call 
    detectLanguage()
    . If the result is 
    null
    or below the confidence threshold, we throw 
    LowConfidenceError
    , and the user sees "Choose the source language manually."
  • Validate. Translating a language into itself is pointless, so we stop with a clear message.
  • Prepare the translator. This is the phase where a language pack may download, so 
    downloadProgress
    updates the progress bar.
  • Translate with streaming. We use 
    translateStreaming()
    and append each chunk to the output. In my test of a four-sentence passage, Chrome returned one chunk per sentence. The docs recommend streaming for longer text. For a short sentence, you get a single chunk, so it behaves the same as 
    translate()
    .

Note that we read the stream with 

getReader()
instead of 
for await
. 
for await
over a 
ReadableStream
needs the 
dom.asynciterable
TypeScript lib, and 
getReader()
works everywhere.

The 

finally
block only resets the UI if this call is still the current one. Without that check, a cancelled older request could reset the state of a newer one.

The 

useEffect
cleanup aborts any pending work and calls 
destroyAll()
when the component unmounts, which releases the models.
